name: Postmodernism
summary: Postmodernism is a late-20th-century philosophical and cultural movement that doubts the grand narratives of modernity, such as progress through reason, Marxist emancipation or religious history, and the claim that knowledge can stand outside language and power. Its thinkers trace how truth, identity and norms are produced by discourse and institutions, and they favor difference, local narratives and dissent over universal consensus. Politically it was taken up mainly on the academic left, in feminism, queer theory, multiculturalism and postcolonial thought.
scope: French post-structuralist and postmodern philosophy of roughly 1968-1995: Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition, Foucault's work on power/knowledge, discipline and sexuality, Derrida's deconstruction and Specters of Marx, with Baudrillard and Deleuze as context, and the political uses of these ideas in postmodern feminism and postcolonial thought. Because it is a philosophy rather than a political program, answers follow the political implications usually drawn by its scholars and academic adherents, and many are low confidence. Postmodernism in art and architecture, Rorty's pragmatism and the Marxist critique of postmodernism (Jameson) are excluded.

sources.usedFor: Derrida's ten plagues of the new world order, the New International, critique of post-1989 liberal triumphalism

universal-healthcare.rationale: Postmodern theory says little about health policy; inferred from the academic-left milieu in which it was received and its concern with inequality, not from its texts.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Not addressed by the core thinkers; inferred from the left-leaning politics of its adherents and Derrida's treatment of underemployment as a plague of the new world order.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Lyotard describes the commodification of knowledge under performativity critically, and Derrida lists the contradictions of the free market among the plagues of post-1989 capitalism.

public-ownership.rationale: Postmodernists criticize capitalism but are equally suspicious of state power and of the Marxist programs that called for nationalization, so no clear answer follows.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Inferred from Derrida's emphasis on unprecedented inequality and the generally left politics of adherents; the core texts do not discuss tax policy.

unions-good.rationale: Not discussed directly; inferred from adherents' left orientation, tempered by their distrust of large organizations claiming to speak for a class.

property-fundamental.rationale: Postmodernism treats rights claims as historically constructed rather than natural, and its thinkers criticize capitalist property relations, so an absolute property right is rejected.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Lyotard warns that multinational corporations are gaining control over information flows that states once governed; inferred support for checking that power.

cut-welfare.rationale: Inferred from adherents' left orientation; Foucault's critique of normalization also makes the 'dependency' framing suspect to them.

worker-ownership.rationale: Some adherents sympathize with self-management, but postmodernism offers no economic program and distrusts emancipatory blueprints of this kind.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Foucault's analysis of the panopticon and disciplinary power treats surveillance as a central technique of domination, and this critique is one of the most widely adopted parts of postmodern thought.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Inferred from Foucault's critique of how institutions define and manage deviance and normality; the core texts do not address drug law.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Adherents' attention to how discourse produces marginalization pulls toward restriction, but their suspicion of state and legal power over discourse pulls the other way.

strong-leader.rationale: Postmodernism is a critique of centralized and totalizing power; a leader who overrides institutions concentrates exactly the authority it distrusts.

state-harmful.rationale: Foucault moves analysis away from the state toward diffuse power, and Derrida calls for a critique of the state, but neither calls for abolishing it; adherents are split.

limit-guns.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the left politics of most adherents.

empower-police-military.rationale: Foucault treats police, prisons and similar institutions as instruments of class power whose hidden violence should be exposed and fought, a view central to his political work.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Inferred from Foucault's critique of the policing of sexuality and the postmodern feminist rejection of a single norm of womanhood.

decide-locally.rationale: Lyotard favors local, heterogeneous language games over universal frameworks; adherents carry this into a preference for local over central authority, though the texts do not discuss administrative levels.

rehabilitation.rationale: Foucault argues the reforming, 'correctional' prison is itself the disciplinary technique that produces delinquency, so adherents reject punishment and rehabilitation alike as framed here.

traditional-family.rationale: Foucault names the family among institutions that maintain class power, and postmodern feminism seeks to destabilize patriarchal norms.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Foucault's history of sexuality underpins queer theory and opposes heteronormativity, though some queer theorists criticize marriage itself as a normalizing institution.

abortion-legal.rationale: Inferred from postmodernism's close association with feminism; the core texts do not address abortion law.

more-religion-public.rationale: Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives explicitly includes Christianity among the grand narratives that no longer legitimate knowledge or society.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Postmodernism became closely linked with multiculturalism, postcolonial thought and legal scholarship that emphasizes racial inequality.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Postmodern feminism, building on Foucault through Judith Butler, rejects a universal female subject and treats gender as produced by discourse and power.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Postmodernists treat national identities as constructed and, in Derrida's words, mythic, and they favor heterogeneity over a protected national tradition.

gradual-change.rationale: Postmodernism distrusts both revolutionary grand narratives and the institutions it seeks to destabilize; deference to established institutions sits worse with it than gradualism does.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Derrida lists the deportation of immigrants and the building of new walls among the ten plagues of the new world order.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Derrida criticizes international law as applied hypocritically against weaker nations yet calls for a transformed international order, so adherents give no clear answer.

free-trade.rationale: Derrida treats economic war and the contradictions of free trade and globalization as plagues; inferred general skepticism of the claim that it benefits everyone.

nation-first.rationale: Derrida's New International unites those who criticize the state and national concepts, and postmodernists reject national identity as a grounding value.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Adherents distrust universalist human-rights justifications and international law that is applied selectively, though some, including Derrida, did not rule intervention out.

open-borders.rationale: Inferred from Derrida's condemnation of deportations and new walls and the postmodern rejection of fixed national identities.

limit-growth.rationale: Inferred from Lyotard's critique of performativity and the rejection of the narrative of progress; the core texts do not address environmental growth limits.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not addressed by the core thinkers; inferred from adherents' left orientation.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Rejecting the Enlightenment narrative of progress through reason and science is central to postmodernism, and Lyotard treats technology as serving performativity rather than emancipation.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Postmodern theory says nothing about nuclear power; Derrida's concern with nuclear weapons does not settle it.

revolution-justified.rationale: Foucault in 1971 accepted the proletariat's violent struggle for power, but postmodernists generally reject the revolutionary grand narrative, so support is qualified.

experts-over-public.rationale: The power/knowledge critique of medicine, psychiatry and expert 'decision makers' is central to the tradition, which treats expert authority as a form of power rather than neutral knowledge.

central-planning.rationale: Postmodernists reject totalizing systems and the Marxist grand narrative that underwrote central planning.

socialized-markets.rationale: Postmodernism offers no economic model and adherents take no common view on market socialism.

land-value-tax.rationale: The tradition has no position on land taxation and nothing in its principles settles it.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Inferred from adherents' left orientation and concern with inequality; not discussed in the core texts.

basic-income.rationale: Derrida says underemployment calls for another concept of work; inferred mild support, not a stated position.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Derrida treats the clash of protectionism and free trade as a contradiction of the market rather than taking a side.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The tradition offers no industrial policy and distrusts both market and state planning.

widespread-small-property.rationale: No position in the core texts, and nothing in postmodern principles settles the distribution of property ownership.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Postmodernists reject utopian end-states of history such as the communist abolition of money as grand narratives, though they criticize commodification.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Inferred from adherents' critique of free-market capitalism; the core texts do not discuss central banking.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Lyotard criticizes systems models that integrate all social actors into one performative whole, and the postmodern preference for dissensus over consensus counts against state-organized class collaboration.

one-party-rule.rationale: Incredulity toward metanarratives such as Marxism is the defining postmodern stance, and many of its founders broke with the French Communist Party; rule by a party with the correct ideology is what it rejects.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Foucault urged political theory to 'cut off the head of the king', and postmodernists reject inherited authority as natural.

democracy-best.rationale: Postmodernists criticize liberal democracy as claiming to have realized history's end, but Derrida and Rorty still affirm a democracy to come or liberal democracy over alternatives.

direct-votes.rationale: Lyotard is skeptical of consensus as a goal, and the tradition takes no stand on referendums versus representation.

workers-councils.rationale: Council communism rests on the class-based grand narrative postmodernists abandoned.

right-to-secede.rationale: Postmodernists value local difference but also treat national and ethnic identities as mythic constructions, so they give no clear answer on secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: Foucault treats human nature as a construct formed within a civilization that serves class power, so claims of natural fitness to rule are what genealogy unmasks.

political-violence-never.rationale: Foucault argued that the proletariat's struggle could involve violence and that 'one makes war to win, not because it is just'.

war-builds-character.rationale: Foucault's account of biopower links modern states to industrial warfare that kills millions, and Derrida treats inter-ethnic and economic wars as plagues.

separate-church-state.rationale: Inferred from the rejection of Christianity as a legitimating metanarrative; adherents are also wary of secularism as a universal narrative.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Scripture as a source of law is a paradigm grand narrative, which postmodernism holds can no longer legitimate social order.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Inferred from adherents' critique of free-market capitalism and of private power such as Derrida's 'phantom states' of organized crime.

military-superiority.rationale: Inferred from the critique of state power, nationalism and the arms trade.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Postmodernism is tied to multiculturalism and postcolonial thought and treats ethnic national identity as a myth; Derrida names inter-ethnic wars driven by it as a plague.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Postmodernists reject Marxism's historical narrative; Foucault's genealogy stresses contingency and replaces ideology with power/knowledge, though he still spoke in class terms in 1971.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Adherents oppose inequality but distrust any single universal standard of equality, favoring heterogeneity; the tradition gives no clear answer.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Inferred from postmodernism's association with postcolonial thought and its critique of Western universalism.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Inferred from postcolonial theory, which grew out of postmodern and poststructuralist thought, and Derrida's view that foreign debt keeps poor countries hungry.

civilizational-union.rationale: Postmodernism rejects totalizing identities and grand narratives such as religion or civilization as foundations of political order.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Postmodernists reject foundational moral claims, including egoism, and offer no settled view either way.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Adherents distrust community norms imposed on individuals as normalizing power, though they also distrust universal rights; inferred.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Postmodernists tend to treat 'nature' as a discursive construct, which cuts against intrinsic value, while some ecological strands affirm it; adherents are split.

limit-population.rationale: Foucault's critique of biopower targets state regulation of populations' births and health; inferred opposition to active population control.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Postmodernism criticizes modernity's progress narrative but does not reject industrial society or wish to return to an earlier one.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Some strands (Deleuze and Guattari's de-territorializing flows) were later read as accelerationist, while Lyotard is wary of technology serving performativity; adherents are split.

human-enhancement.rationale: Foucault urged experimentation with subjectivity and postmodernists reject a fixed human nature; inferred openness to self-transformation.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Lyotard describes the handing of regulation to machines and performativity criteria critically, as a threat to the legitimation of knowledge and justice.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Inferred from the critique of surveillance and of state control over information; Lyotard asks who will decide which channels and data are forbidden.

restore-past-order.rationale: Postmodernism rejects narratives of a lost origin or presence as much as narratives of progress, and Foucault's genealogy shows past orders were contingent rather than natural.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Lyotard criticizes legitimation by performance and efficiency, though adherents also distrust ideology; inferred.

missingStatements.text: Claims to objective knowledge are shaped by the interests of those in power.
missingStatements.rationale: The inseparability of knowledge and power is a founding claim of Lyotard and Foucault and the core of the postmodern critique.

missingStatements.text: There are universal truths about morality and society that hold across all cultures.
missingStatements.rationale: Postmodernism is defined by its rejection of universal, foundational truths and grand narratives in favor of local, plural ones.

notes: Postmodern thinkers rarely stated policy positions, so most economic and many social answers are inferred from the left politics of the movement's academic adherents and marked low. Foucault's views shifted (more Marxist in 1971, closer to ethics and interest in liberalism late in life), and Rorty's 'postmodernist bourgeois liberalism' would answer several governance questions more favorably to liberal democracy and markets. Critics such as Habermas and Chomsky charge the tradition with relativism; adherents dispute that label.
